measurement.happened:
This week in DR Congo was dominated by a terrifying convergence of two crises: a massive Ebola outbreak and renewed armed violence in the east, compounded by a web of mining disputes and political maneuvering.

Ebola was the single biggest story. The outbreak has now killed more than 5,300 people, with a fatality rate topping 50 percent according to Bloomberg. The World Health Organization gave the green light to clinical trials of two new Ebola vaccines, and Médecins Sans Frontières issued an urgent appeal to widen access to the existing Ervebo vaccine. The human toll was made painfully visible when a British doctor who tested positive in Congo was evacuated to London for treatment, and Ebola survivors were filmed comforting sick children in isolation wards. The outbreak also intersected with the security crisis: IS-linked Islamist militants raided a village in North Kivu, killing at least 33 people and forcing Ebola patients to flee their treatment facilities, a scene captured in a TV5Monde video report. A cholera epidemic running in parallel has already claimed 1,800 lives since the start of the year, according to the WHO, and an anthrax outbreak that killed hippos in Virunga National Park has prompted authorities to warn of possible transmission to humans. The health system is stretched to breaking point, with overcrowded classrooms and food insecurity making the population more vulnerable.

In the security sphere, the 33-killing village attack by IS-linked militants (reported by AP, Al Jazeera, Reuters, and TV5Monde) was the most violent single event of the week. Residents of Uvira in South Kivu told TV5Monde they live in a state of 'psychose' and fear a return of full-scale war. Armed groups are also taxing beer transporters on the roads, squeezing local commerce. The broader context includes ongoing US sanctions on Rwanda tied to the Congo war, as discussed in a BBC broadcast, and the DRC-Rwanda tension that colored the Francophonie organization's leadership election.

On the minerals and mining front, a busy week of disputes unfolded. The Congo government opened a fraud inquiry after seizing copper and cobalt shipments it deemed illegally mined. Residents filed a lawsuit against a Chinese copper mine over alleged pollution. Kinshasa told China's Huayou Cobalt that its unit must pay six million dollars in compensation despite a project halt. The country also said the US minerals deal should be judged by actual projects on the ground rather than signed agreements, signaling a more pragmatic posture. Bloomberg reported that Trafigura-led creditors took a 70 percent loss on a Congolese miner's debt, and the government is now seeking twelve billion dollars in investor money to fix chronic power shortages. The Lobito Corridor, a major port-to-port logistics project, remains largely unknown to the communities it is supposed to serve, according to a TV5Monde video.

Politically, the Senate definitively adopted a controversial referendum law, closing out a long parliamentary saga. The opposition C64 alliance was warned its leaders could be arrested for meeting with former president Joseph Kabila, a move that reads as a power play. The Francophonie election took place under the shadow of the DRC-Rwanda rivalry. The US and DRC signaled they would accelerate economic cooperation and investment, per a BBC broadcast in Kirundi.

A lighter note: a teenager from conflict-hit Congo made history at the Youth Olympics, competing with his father as coach, a small story of resilience amid the chaos.
measurement.expected:
Ebola will almost certainly remain the dominant story next week. With the fatality rate above 50 percent, over 5,300 confirmed deaths, and the militant raid on an Ebola ward still fresh, expect the WHO and MSF to issue updated case counts, likely showing further increases. The two new vaccine clinical trials will move into early enrollment, and there will be more foreign healthcare worker evacuations or quarantines. The intersection of Ebola and armed violence in North Kivu will generate at least one more dramatic incident or appeal. Confidence: almost certain.

Armed violence in eastern Congo is probable to continue. The ADF and other IS-linked groups will likely carry out at least one more attack in North Kivu or South Kivu, and the Uvira corridor will see either renewed fighting or a tense standoff. The military may announce a small operation or a change of command in the east. The beer-transporter taxation by armed groups will either escalate into a local dispute or be quietly absorbed. Confidence: probable.

The mining and minerals disputes will keep generating headlines. The fraud inquiry into the seized copper and cobalt will produce at least one arrest or one formal charge. The Huayou compensation saga will see a new legal filing or a government press statement. The twelve-billion-dollar power investment search will attract at least one named investor or a round of preliminary meetings. The US minerals deal will see a technical working group meeting or a statement from the State Department. Confidence: probable.

The anthrax alert from Virunga is possible to develop into a confirmed human case or a broader livestock culling announcement, which would add another layer to the already strained health system. Confidence: possible.

Politically, the newly adopted referendum law will trigger either a presidential decree setting a date or a fresh round of opposition protests and C64 statements. The threat of arresting C64 leaders for meeting Kabila may materialize into one or two actual detentions, creating a small political crisis. The DRC-Rwanda tension will keep simmering in the background of any diplomatic event. Confidence: possible to probable.

The cholera toll will keep climbing, and the WHO will likely update its figure above 1,800. The Lobito Corridor will remain a low-visibility infrastructure story unless a new contract or community protest surfaces. Confidence: possible.

Less likely surprises: a sudden ceasefire or power-sharing proposal between Kinshasa and Kigali; a major military offensive in the east that shifts the front line; a new Ebola cluster in a previously unaffected province like Haut-Katanga; a constitutional court ruling on the referendum law within the week; a high-profile resignation in the cabinet.

Things I would not bet on: a full-scale civil war declaration; the Ebola outbreak being declared over; a major earthquake or volcanic event; the Senate reversing the referendum law; a new US-led peacekeeping mission being announced; the Lobito Corridor reaching a major construction milestone; a change of president; a successful coup attempt.

delta.motion:
Eight days apart, these two photographs show a country whose crises have not simply continued but have layered onto each other in ways the first image did not fully reveal. Ebola remains the gravitational center, but its story has broadened: the death toll climbed from just over 5,000 to more than 5,300, the WHO formally greenlit clinical trials of two new vaccines (up from a single three-shot trial in early stages), and Médecins Sans Frontières issued an urgent appeal for wider Ervebo access. What was a single-disease story in the first photograph has become a multi-disease health emergency: a cholera epidemic that has already killed 1,800 people this year now runs in parallel, and an anthrax outbreak in Virunga National Park has killed hippos and prompted warnings about human transmission. The health system is not just strained by Ebola; it is being hit from three directions at once.

Security violence shifted in character. In the first photograph, the military narrative was dominated by Kabila's FRN movement and the M23 conflict, with the US sanctions on Rwanda as the headline. In the second, the most violent single event is an IS-linked militant raid on a village in North Kivu that killed at least 33 people and forced Ebola patients to flee their treatment facilities. The ADF, which in the first photo was a background story about gold smuggling, has become the face of the violence. Kabila's FRN, which was a major standalone story, has receded in visibility; Kabila now appears more as a political target (the C64 opposition was warned its leaders could be arrested for meeting him) than as an active rebel commander on the ground. Uvira residents describe living in a state of 'psychose,' but no new FRN offensive has materialized in the coverage.

The mining and minerals sector grew from a couple of discrete stories into a dense cluster of legal, financial, and diplomatic disputes. The first photograph had the suspension of the artisanal mining agency head and a Gates-backed company complaining about China. The second shows a fraud inquiry after the government seized copper and cobalt shipments, a resident lawsuit against a Chinese copper mine over pollution, a demand that Huayou Cobalt pay six million dollars in compensation, the US minerals deal being reframed as something to be judged by actual projects rather than signed agreements, Trafigura-led creditors taking a 70 percent loss on a Congolese miner's debt, and the government seeking twelve billion dollars in investor money to fix chronic power shortages. The Lobito Corridor logistics project also surfaced, with communities it is supposed to serve saying they know little about it. The sector has gone from 'one agency head suspended' to a multi-front legal and financial confrontation.

Politically, the referendum law moved from 'adopted without opposition, sparking a firestorm' to 'definitively adopted by the Senate,' closing the parliamentary saga. The C64 opposition went from meeting in Rome and calling for dialogue to being warned its leaders could be arrested for meeting Kabila. The Francophonie leadership election appeared as a new arena where the DRC-Rwanda rivalry played out. The US and DRC signaled they would accelerate economic cooperation, a positive note that sat alongside the ongoing sanctions on Rwanda.

What vanished: the FATF grey-list removal disappeared entirely, as expected. Tshisekedi's FIFA connection and the Ash Dykes expedition story are gone. The specific Sentry report on gold smuggling funding the ADF as a standalone piece has merged into the broader mining cluster. The US sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry, which was a fresh headline, is now referenced as ongoing context in a BBC broadcast. The one small positive of treatment centres discharging patients, noted in the first photo, does not appear in the second.

What appeared that was not in the first photograph: the cholera epidemic, the anthrax outbreak, the 33-kill IS-linked village raid, the British doctor evacuated to London, armed groups taxing beer transporters, the Lobito Corridor, the Trafigura debt loss, the $12B power investment push, the Francophonie election, the US-DRC economic cooperation signal, and the Youth Olympics teenager story. The overall motion is from a set of distinct, somewhat separable crises toward a more tangled, overlapping picture where health, security, mining, and politics are no longer separate columns but a single knot.
delta.wind:
EBOLA. The expectation was almost certain to remain the dominant story, and it was. The expectation that the death toll would cross 6,000 or 7,000 was only partially met: the toll reached just over 5,300, which is climbing but slower than the 'growing exponentially' language suggested. The expectation of more neighbouring countries tightening borders or announcing cases was not clearly confirmed in the second photograph; the Kenya and Nigeria cases from the first week did not generate new headlines about further spread. The expectation of at least one more attack on a medical team by community mobs was not the form the violence took; instead, IS-linked militants raided a village and forced Ebola patients to flee, which is a different threat vector. The vaccine story grew faster than expected: the first photo mentioned a three-shot trial in early stages, and by the second the WHO had greenlit two new vaccine trials and MSF was issuing urgent appeals for Ervebo access. The 'small silver lining' of treatment centres discharging patients faded from the coverage. The biggest miss was the parallel cholera epidemic and the anthrax outbreak, neither of which was in the expectation. The expectation treated Ebola as a single-disease story; reality made it a multi-disease health emergency.

RWANDA-CONGO TENSIONS AND KABILA/FRN. The expectation was that Rwanda would respond to the US sanctions, that Tshisekedi would keep calling Kabila a puppet, and that a new battle or skirmish in the east was probable while a major offensive was possible. The sanctions are now referenced as ongoing context rather than a fresh provocation, so Kigali's response was either quieter than expected or absorbed into the broader diplomatic noise. Tshisekedi's 'supplétif' language is not explicitly repeated in the second photo, but the C64-arrest warning for meeting Kabila is a different and arguably sharper escalation against the opposition rather than a direct Tshisekedi-Kabila exchange. The new battle was probable, and violence did come, but it was IS-linked ADF militants in North Kivu, not the FRN or M23. The FRN as a distinct armed movement receded in the coverage. A major offensive by the FRN did not materialize in the headlines. The expectation over-indexed on the Kabila/FRN axis as the primary military threat and under-weighted the IS-linked insurgency as the actual violence generator. The Francophonie election as a new arena for DRC-Rwanda rivalry was not in the expectation at all.

OPPOSITION AND REFERENDUM LAW. The expectation was a C64 joint statement from Rome, visible protests, a general strike as possible, and a constitutional crisis as unlikely. The C64 Rome statement is not explicitly mentioned in the second photo. Protests are not in the coverage. The general strike did not happen, consistent with the 'unlikely' rating. The constitutional crisis did not happen, also consistent. What did happen was the Senate definitively adopting the referendum law, which closes the saga rather than fuelling ongoing protest, and the C64-arrest warning, which is a new and sharper move than the expectation anticipated. The expectation framed the opposition as the active actor pushing back; reality shows the government consolidating (Senate adoption) and threatening (arrest warning) while the opposition is on the defensive.

GOLD, MINING, ADF. The expectation was a replacement appointment of the mining agency head, government inspections, and a possible major crackdown or new smuggling route. The replacement appointment is not mentioned. The inspections angle shows up as the fraud inquiry on seized copper and cobalt. The 'major crackdown' broadened into a multi-front legal and financial cluster: the lawsuit against a Chinese mine, the Huayou compensation demand, the Trafigura debt loss, the $12B power investment push, and the Lobito Corridor. The ADF-gold-smuggling link as a standalone Sentry report faded, but the ADF as a violence actor grew. The expectation treated the mining story as a regulatory and smuggling issue; reality showed it as a legal, financial, and diplomatic multi-front dispute involving China, the US, European creditors, and local communities.

FATF. Expected to be a footnote. It vanished entirely. Correct.

CHINA MINING. Expected slow-burn friction. It became a multi-front dispute with a lawsuit, a compensation demand, and a broader 'judge us by projects' posture. The friction grew faster and wider than the 'slow-burn' framing suggested.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES. The ADF launching a major attack on a mining site or releasing a video was in the 'less likely' list; the 33-kill village raid is close to that and it happened. A new Ebola case in a third or fourth country was listed as less likely; it does not clearly appear in the second photo. A surprise Tshisekedi-Kabila meeting was listed as less likely; it did not happen, but the C64-arrest warning for meeting Kabila is a related development. A new US or EU sanctions package on Congolese officials was listed as less likely; instead, the US and DRC signaled accelerated economic cooperation, which is the opposite direction.

THINGS NOT BET ON. None of the 'would not bet on' items happened, which is consistent. No civil war declaration, no Ebola halt, no new peace deal, no FATF reversal, no volcanic eruption, no Tshisekedi removal, no vaccine approval and rollout, no C64 general strike, no oil or copper price shock. The expectation's negative space was largely correct.

What this says about the way expectations have been wrong for this country: The expectation treated the crises as somewhat separable tracks (Ebola, Rwanda-Kabila, opposition, mining, FATF, China) that could be assessed independently. Reality showed them as a single overlapping system where an IS-linked raid displaces Ebola patients, a cholera epidemic competes for the same overwhelmed health workers, a mining fraud inquiry intersects with a Chinese lawsuit and a US minerals deal, and a Senate referendum vote is entangled with an opposition arrest warning and a Francophonie election. The expectation also over-weighted the Kabila/FRN axis as the primary military threat and under-weighted the IS-linked ADF. It under-weighted the parallel cholera and anthrax crises. It framed the mining story as a regulatory issue when it is actually a multi-stakeholder legal and financial confrontation. And it missed the Francophonie as a new diplomatic arena entirely. The expectation was structured around the first photograph's headlines; the second photograph shows a country where the headlines have reorganized around the intersections rather than the individual stories.
delta.driver: The force pushing DR Congo from the first photograph to the second is the simultaneous compounding of multiple crises in a country whose health system, eastern provinces, mining economy, and political institutions are all already fragile, and whose government is trying to project control while the ground reality deteriorates on every axis at once. Ebola is the gravitational center, but it is no longer a single disease: cholera and anthrax are running in parallel, straining the same hospitals, the same health workers, the same community trust that is already fractured by attacks on medical teams. The security situation in the east has shifted from a proxy war framed around M23 and the FRN to a more diffuse and violent landscape where IS-linked ADF militants are the primary killers, armed groups tax beer transporters, and residents of Uvira describe living in a state of 'psychose.' The mining sector, which funds much of the eastern conflict and the national budget, is under multi-front legal and financial pressure from the government's own fraud inquiries, Chinese mining disputes, European creditor losses, and a push to attract twelve billion dollars for power infrastructure, all while the US minerals deal is being reframed as something to be judged by actual projects rather than signed agreements. Politically, Tshisekedi's camp is consolidating: the referendum law is now definitively adopted, the C64 opposition is under arrest warnings for meeting Kabila, and the Francophonie election has become another arena where the DRC-Rwanda rivalry plays out. The US is pulling in two directions at once, sanctioning Rwanda's defence ministry while signaling accelerated economic cooperation with Congo. The result is a country being squeezed from health, security, economy, and politics simultaneously, with each crisis feeding the others and the government trying to manage all four fronts with an overstretched apparatus. The motion from photo one to photo two is not a single event but the acceleration of a convergence: the crises that were running in parallel in the first photograph have begun to interact, displace each other's resources, and create a more tangled and less legible picture than any single headline can capture.

Politics moved from opposition pushing back to government consolidating and threatening. The overall direction is convergence, not divergence.

The wind tells me where I have been wrong: I over-weighted the Kabila/FRN axis as the primary military threat and under-weighted the IS-linked ADF. I treated Ebola as a single-disease story when reality made it a multi-disease emergency. I framed mining as a regulatory issue when it is actually a legal and financial multi-front dispute. I missed the Francophonie as a diplomatic arena. I treated crises as separable tracks when they interact. I over-read 'exponential' language in the death toll trajectory; the actual climb has been steadier. The correction is to think in terms of intersections and interactions, not parallel tracks.

What I would not bet on: a full-scale FRN offensive (Kabila is more political target than military actor right now); Ebola being declared contained or a new vaccine approved and rolled out (trials just started, it is too early); a C64 general strike (the opposition is on the defensive, not mobilizing); a coup or Tshisekedi's removal (the government is consolidating, not fracturing); a new peace deal (the violence is IS-linked, not a bilateral negotiation); a major copper or cobalt price shock (the disputes are legal, not market-moving yet); a volcanic eruption or natural disaster. crystal.eli5:
Imagine a country where three different emergencies are happening at the same time, in the same hospitals, with the same doctors and nurses. That is DR Congo right now. Ebola has killed more than 5,300 people, but it is not the only disease: cholera has killed 1,800 people this year, and a germ that killed hippos in a national park is now being watched because it might jump to humans. All three diseases are fighting for the same small number of beds, the same small number of health workers, and the same community trust that is already shaky because armed groups keep attacking villages.

In the eastern part of the country, a group of fighters linked to the Islamic State has been the main source of violence. Last week they raided a village and killed 33 people, and some of the people who ran for help were Ebola patients leaving a treatment center. This is the kind of thing that makes the crises feel like one big mess instead of separate problems. The former president, Kabila, is still a big political figure, but he is more of a target the government is angry at than a general leading an army. The real killing is being done by the IS-linked fighters.

The economy is tangled up in all of this. The government seized some copper and cobalt that it thinks was mined illegally, and now there is a fraud investigation. A Chinese mining company is being sued by local residents over pollution. Another Chinese company is being told to pay six million dollars. A European group of lenders lost 70 percent of their money on a Congolese mining company. And the government is asking investors for twelve billion dollars to fix the power grid, which is a huge number. All of this is happening while the United States is sanctioning Rwanda's military but also telling Congo it wants to invest more money there. It is a lot of threads pulled in different directions at the same time.

Politically, the government has been winning. The Senate voted to make a controversial referendum law official, which closes that chapter. But the opposition group called C64 has been warned that its leaders could be arrested just for meeting with the former president. So next week, we might see either actual arrests or a very angry public speech from the opposition. The government is trying to look in control while the ground reality is getting more tangled.

The most important thing to watch is not any single story but the way the stories bump into each other. An ADF raid that also kicks up a cholera treatment center. A mining dispute that turns into a protest in a village already hit by Ebola. A new vaccine trial milestone that gets overshadowed by another village attack. judgment.comparison: Both forecasts are remarkably similar in structure, coverage, and accuracy. They both correctly identified Ebola as the dominant story, the violence in the east (though both misidentified the specific actor as FRN rather than IS-linked militants), the DRC-Rwanda tension, the C64 friction, the mining/China economics, and the US sanctions. Both slightly overestimated the Ebola death toll (predicting 6,000+ against an actual 5,300+). Both missed the same secondary stories: the cholera epidemic (1,800 deaths), the anthrax/hippos in Virunga, the $12 billion power investment push, the Trafigura 70% loss, the Francophonie election, and the US-DRC economic cooperation acceleration. Both got the C64 and referendum law dynamics right, with the law being definitively adopted and the opposition facing an arrest warning. Both correctly treated the FATF removal as a footnote. The differences are minor: B's vaccine trial framing is slightly closer to the actual WHO green-lighting of two new vaccine trials; B's 'second deadliest in history' language matches the Bloomberg fatality-rate headline; A's structured 'less likely surprises' and 'things I would not bet on' sections are marginally more useful for a reader calibrating probability; A's 'at least one more attack on a medical team' is slightly more specific and aligns a bit better with the raid that forced Ebola patients to flee. B's Uganda quarantine prediction was a specific miss, while A did not make that specific call. B's not-bet-on section listed a London Ebola case as 'still a stretch,' which the British doctor evacuation partially contradicted, while A listed it as a 'less likely surprise,' which is a similar level of skepticism. Neither forecast captured the full health-system stress (cholera, anthrax, overcrowded classrooms, food insecurity) that the week's reporting revealed as a parallel crisis. In terms of serving a reader, both would have given a solid mental map of the week: Ebola dominant, violence in the east, political friction, mining disputes, DRC-Rwanda tension.
